claims.text: Increasing atomic-size mismatch in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles reduces their high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
Greater atomic-size mismatch causes phase segregation or chemical ordering to begin at lower temperatures.
Multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles can initially exist as homogeneous high-entropy solid solutions.
A PtPdCoCuNi-type nanoparticle can serve as the homogeneous initial alloy system.
Replacing a constituent with an isovalent atom of larger radius will systematically increase the alloy's atomic-size mismatch.
The proposed elemental substitution isolates atomic-size mismatch from competing chemical or thermodynamic effects.
The ranges 773–1173 K and 473–1923 K are relevant to catalytic and thermoelectric service, respectively.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes generate localized lattice strain or severe lattice distortion.
Size-mismatch-induced lattice strain enhances atomic diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion caused by lattice strain promotes early segregation or chemical ordering.
Configurational entropy stabilizes a single solid-solution phase against intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch raises energetic inhomogeneity in the alloy.
Strain-induced energetic inhomogeneity lowers the threshold for diffusion and elemental segregation.
Competition between entropy-driven stabilization and strain-induced ordering determines the onset of segregation or ordering.
The increased-mismatch nanoparticles will show diffraction or compositional-mapping evidence of segregation or ordering at a lower temperature than the control.
The original, minimally mismatched nanoparticles will retain single-phase behavior to higher temperatures than the modified nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: Replacing one element changes chemical identity and alloy composition, whereas the conditions state that composition aside from atomic-size variation remains constant. Thus the intervention does not cleanly vary only atomic size.

A near-equiatomic PtPdCoCuNi example nominally contains two noble-metal constituents, approximately 40 at% in total if exactly equiatomic, which is in tension with the repeated requirement for low noble-metal content.
